nodes.label: Source Is Read-Only in a Migration
nodes.rationale: Every statement a migration sends to the source is a SELECT, which makes rollback trivial: point the application back at the source and nothing has been lost. The promise was deliberately narrowed from 'the source is never written to' when the management panel arrived, because the app as a whole can now administer any registered server and saying otherwise would be untrue.

nodes.label: Failure Leaves the Target Untouched
nodes.rationale: The truncate, the copy, the sequence fixup and the verification share one transaction; if any fails, the rollback leaves the target byte-identical to what it was before the run. There is never a half-migrated state to clean up.

nodes.label: Success Means the Data Actually Moved
nodes.rationale: A run only exits successfully if the copy plan was non-empty, at least one row was copied, every table's row count matches the source, and no foreign key has an orphaned child row. Any of those failing is a failure, not a warning. FKs are re-checked because constraint triggers are suspended during the copy.

nodes.label: The Escape Hatches (Relaxable Checks)
nodes.rationale: Four checks can be turned off — allow tables missing from target, allow schema risk, allow collation mismatch, verify only. All are off by default, each exists because a real migration occasionally needs it, and each says what it lets through. Turning one on without reading what it reported cancels the reason the tool exists.

nodes.label: ORM Migration History Is the Target's and Is Kept
nodes.rationale: History tables (__EFMigrationsHistory, django_migrations, schema_migrations, flyway_schema_history, __drizzle_migrations) describe the target, not the data being moved, so they are neither truncated nor filled. Copying the source's rows replaces a true statement with a false one: EF finds no baseline record, re-applies it, and fails on existing tables — a real failure this tool once caused. Mirroring never creates a history table, and copying history anyway is an explicit overwrite option, not a relaxed check.

nodes.label: CASCADE Closure Computed Before Locks
nodes.rationale: TRUNCATE ... RESTART IDENTITY CASCADE reaches every target table referencing one being copied; the affected set is computed from the target's foreign keys and listed during pre-flight, before the transaction opens. The check also proves history-table preservation: if a preserved table falls inside the cascade closure the run fails, naming the table and the foreign-key path — a guarantee is not built on 'safe in practice, unverified in principle'.

nodes.label: Server Management Panel (No Migration Guarantees)
nodes.rationale: A different tool that happens to live in the same window: nothing is transactional, nothing reversible. Instead: a drop names its cost first, only proceeds when the object's name is typed back (checked server-side too), system objects are refused outright, closing other sessions is opt-in, blocked deletes explain themselves and offer ownership reassignment, and the server's own error DETAIL is shown verbatim.

nodes.label: Stored Credentials (Machine-Keyed DataProtection)
nodes.rationale: Saved connections live in a local JSON file with passwords encrypted via ASP.NET Core data-protection keys scoped to the machine — the file is not portable. This protects the file at rest and against accidental commits, not against someone already logged in as the user, because the app must decrypt to connect.

nodes.label: Generated Passwords Exist Only in the PDF
nodes.rationale: Per-database passwords are generated in memory, written into the PDF report, and held only until the process exits — never stored in the connections file, a log or a temp file. Nobody can recover them from the machine, including the user: if the report is lost the password must be reset with ALTER ROLE. The PDF is a credential.

nodes.label: Identifier Quoting per Product
nodes.rationale: No SQL dialect accepts a bound parameter where an identifier goes, so names from the browser are quoted for their product (double-quote doubled for PostgreSQL, bracket doubled for SQL Server) and rejected if they carry a control character. A SQL Server collation name sits in a keyword position and cannot be quoted, so it is validated against letters, digits and underscores instead.
